question:
Client: Mrs. Lakshmi Devi. Matter: motor accident claim, death of spouse.

Her husband was killed in a road accident involving a commercial truck. The truck driver was operating the vehicle without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies the claim, arguing the policy is void because the driver was unlicensed, and that it bears no liability.

Key facts: deceased aged 42; monthly income Rs 35,000; dependants are the wife and two minor children (8 and 12); the truck was a commercial vehicle owned by a transport company; the driver held no valid licence; the insurer contests liability.

Research the corpus and advise on supporting precedents, adverse precedents, and strategy.

prove a breach of the policy, but the said breach is not a fundamental breach or the breach did not

payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.court: Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, Madhugiri
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.
payload.ratio: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party under the Motor Vehicles Act regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence, and the mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of its third-party liability.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
payload.ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.

payload.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
payload.court: Supreme Court of India
payload.holding: The Supreme Court held that the principles laid down in Swaran Singh's case regarding third-party risks have no application to non-third-party claims such as own-damage claims, and that a fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
payload.ratio: The decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 and does not extend to own-damage claims or disputes between the insurer and the insured where no third party is involved.

19. We have considered over the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the parties.
20. In Susamma Thomas case the Hon'ble Apex Court has held that the determination of quantum
of compensation must answer what contemporary society "would deem to be a fair sum such as
would allow the wrong-doer to hold up his head among his neighbours and say with their approval
that he has done the fair thing". The amount awarded must not be niggardly since the "law values
life and limb in a free society in generous scales". All this means that the sum awarded must be fair
and reasonable by accepted legal standards.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi for death of spouse (aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants) involving a commercial truck driven without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a light motor vehicle as a commercial vehicle. The insurer must pay the third party and may recover from the insured if there was a breach.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim of a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab/taxi). The driver held an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to pay third-party compensation despite the licence defect.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent from the Supreme Court. It establishes that even where the driver's licence does not match the vehicle class (commercial vehicle), the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 remains intact. The insurer must pay and can only seek recovery from the owner.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of the offending tempo did not possess a valid driving licence. The Delhi High Court held the insurer statutorily liable to pay the third-party claimants and recover from the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly on point: the driver had no valid licence at all. The court confirmed that even a fundamental breach (invalid licence) does not defeat the third party's right to recover from the insurer. The insurer must pay first and then recover.
supporting.quote: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held only an LMV licence and lacked the badge/authorisation to drive a tourist Maxi Cab (commercial transport vehicle). The Madras High Court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is factually very close: a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) driven by someone without the proper licence class. The court ordered pay-and-recover, confirming the insurer's liability to the third party.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV/transport vehicle licence but not a heavy goods vehicle endorsement. The Madras High Court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the principle that licence class mismatch does not absolve the insurer of third-party liability. The court specifically rejected the insurer's argument that even pay-and-recover cannot be ordered.
supporting.quote: When the driver of the vehicle involved in the accident did not have a valid driving licence, whether the insurer can be directed to pay compensation to the Claimants and recover the same subsequently from the insured... [Answer: Yes].

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor and recover from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench of Karnataka High Court held that even fundamental breach does not defeat third-party rights. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench decision that comprehensively analyses the law. It confirms that the rule of pay-and-recover applies even for fundamental breaches, and the only exception is fraud/collusion between the victim and insured — which is not present here.
supporting.quote: The rule of pay and recover is applicable in view of the mandate in Section 149(4) of the Act and even if there is a breach of the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer is bound to satisfy the judgment and award as if it were a judgment debtor.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must pay the third party first and recover from the owner under the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The Tribunal found a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover to protect the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even in the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — the Tribunal ordered pay-and-recover. This is the worst-case scenario for the claimant on facts, and the court still protected the third party.
supporting.quote: The petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a special endorsement required for the vehicle type (hazardous goods), the insurer cannot escape liability to third parties but has a right to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for driving a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The Punjab & Haryana High Court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the licence defect is specific to the vehicle's use (commercial goods vehicle), the insurer's liability to third parties remains intact with recovery rights.
supporting.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident. The Tribunal held the insurer liable, finding that non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: Distinguishes between 'no licence' and 'licence expired' — but the broader principle that statutory liability to third parties overrides policy conditions is directly applicable.
supporting.quote: The liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: Multiplier must be based on deceased's age (not claimants'), future prospects apply to self-employed persons, and courts must award just compensation even without cross-appeal.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was 23 (here 42), self-employed. The court applied Sarla Verma multiplier table and Pranay Sethi future prospects percentages.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the quantum framework. For a 42-year-old self-employed deceased with 3 dependants: multiplier 14, future prospects 25%, 1/3rd deduction. This directly governs the compensation calculation.
supporting.quote: The multiplier to be used should be as mentioned in Column (4) of the table... which starts with an operative multiplier of 18... M-14 for 41 to 45 years.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited to third-party claims. However, our client IS a third party, so this judgment actually supports us — it confirms Swaran Singh applies to third-party claims. The insurer may try to use the 'fake licence' discussion to argue that if the licence is fake (not just absent), different considerations apply.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment expressly limits its holding to non-third-party (own-damage) claims. It states: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client's claim is a third-party death claim, squarely within Swaran Singh's ambit. The 'fake licence' discussion is obiter for third-party claims and distinguishable — here the driver had no licence at all, not a fake one.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger travels in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and pay-and-recover cannot be ordered.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available in all cases. However, this case is about passengers in a private vehicle for hire — a fundamentally different category from a third-party road user killed by a commercial truck.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns gratuitous passengers in a private vehicle — persons whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. Our client is a third-party road user (the deceased was not a passenger in the offending vehicle). The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and S.Iyyapan has consistently held that third-party victims are entitled to recover from the insurer regardless of licence breaches. This judgment is inapplicable.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4)/(5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is a limited remedy. But again, this concerns gratuitous passengers, not third-party road users.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The deceased was not a gratuitous passenger in the offending vehicle. He was a third-party road user (pedestrian/other vehicle occupant) killed by a commercial truck. The statutory requirement to insure third-party risks under Section 147 is mandatory and the insurer's liability to third parties is well-established. This judgment is confined to its facts.

adverse.title: Shivlal And Ors. Etc. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is not liable for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle where the risk is not statutorily required to be covered.
adverse.risk_to_client: Irrelevant to our facts — this is about gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles under the 1939 Act.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is about gratuitous passengers in a tractor-trolley, not about a third-party road user killed by a commercial vehicle. The legal framework (1939 Act) and the factual matrix are entirely different. No adverse inference can be drawn.

adverse.title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
adverse.principle: Where a tractor is used for non-agricultural purposes in violation of the insurance policy, the insurer is not liable.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that policy breaches can absolve the insurer. However, this case is about a use-restriction breach (agricultural vs non-agricultural use), not a licence breach. The legal principle is different.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a use-restriction breach (tractor used for construction instead of agriculture), not a driving licence defect. The line of Supreme Court authorities (Swaran Singh, S.Iyyapan, Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba) specifically governs licence-related breaches and mandates pay-and-recover for third-party claims. This judgment is distinguishable.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh And Ors.
adverse.principle: Only legal representatives who were dependent upon the victim at the time of death are entitled to compensation under 'loss of dependency'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if any of the three dependants (wife, children aged 8 and 12) are not actually dependent, their claim under loss of dependency should be reduced. However, the wife and minor children are clearly dependents.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The wife and two minor children (aged 8 and 12) are unquestionably dependents. This judgment actually supports our position by confirming that genuine dependents are entitled to loss of dependency. The insurer cannot argue that minor children or a non-earning spouse are non-dependent.

priority_arguments: 1. STATUTORY LIABILITY TO THIRD PARTIES: The insurer's liability under Section 149 MV Act to third-party victims is statutory and cannot be defeated by a breach of policy conditions. Lead with S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and Satto (doc_033) — both hold that even where the driver had no valid licence, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.

2. PAY-AND-RECOVER IS THE ESTABLISHED REMEDY: Even if the insurer proves a fundamental breach (no licence), the consistent line of authority from the Supreme Court and High Courts mandates pay-and-recover. Cite Yallavva (doc_025, Full Bench), V.Vijayakumar (doc_035), Chennamma (doc_027), and Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024).

3. BURDEN OF PROOF ON INSURER: The insurer must prove by cogent evidence that (a) the driver had no licence, AND (b) the owner was aware or complicit in the breach. Mere absence of a licence does not automatically absolve the insurer — the breach must be on the part of the insured (owner), not just the driver. Cite Swaran Singh principles as applied in Satto (doc_033).

4. QUANTUM: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, Rs 35,000/month, 3 dependants. Apply Sarla Verma multiplier of 14, future prospects at 25% (Pranay Sethi), 1/3rd deduction. Compute using the framework from Surendra Singh (doc_019). Estimated compensation: ~Rs 51 lakhs plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a.

5. NO COLLUSION OR FRAUD: The Full Bench in Yallavva (doc_025) held that the only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured. There is none here — the deceased was an innocent third-party road user.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition until realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 → Annual Rs 4,20,000. Future prospects +25% (self-employed, age 42) → Rs 5,25,000. Less 1/3rd personal expenses (3 dependants) → Rs 3,50,000. Multiplier 14 (age 42) → Rs 49,00,000. Conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 159,720 (wife) + parental consortium Rs 159,720 (2 minor children) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. Range reflects potential variation in future prospects percentage if employment status is disputed.
risks: The insurer may argue that the driver had no licence at all (not merely a mismatch of licence class), which some Tribunals have treated as a more serious breach. However, even in Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) where the driver had NO licence, pay-and-recover was ordered.

The insurer may argue that the owner (transport company) was complicit in allowing an unlicensed driver to operate a commercial vehicle, making this a 'conscious breach'. However, the consistent Supreme Court position is that even conscious/wilful breach does not defeat third-party rights — the insurer still pays and recovers (Satto doc_033, citing Lehru).
Risk that the Tribunal may reduce the multiplier or future prospects if the deceased's employment status (self-employed vs permanent) is disputed. Ensure documentary proof of income is produced.
The insurer may challenge the quantum by arguing that the income of Rs 35,000/month is not adequately proved. Ensure salary slips, bank statements, or income tax returns are available.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is jointly and severally liable to pay the awarded compensation, with liberty to the insurer to recover the same from the owner/insured in separate proceedings. Alternatively, seek a direct pay-and-recover order. Given the clear line of authority, the claimant should also seek an order for interim compensation under Section 140 MV Act (no-fault liability) which is payable regardless of licence issues.

caveats: The corpus does not contain the Constitution Bench judgment in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 itself, though it is cited extensively in multiple judgments. The principles from Swaran Singh are well-established through the cited authorities.

The corpus does not contain Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba (2018) 3 SCC 208, which is cited in doc_024 and doc_001 as authority for pay-and-recover even where the insurer succeeds in its defence. The principle is nevertheless available through the cited cases.

The corpus does not contain any judgment specifically about the quantum of consortium for minor children (parental consortium) under the post-Pranay Sethi framework, though the compute_quantum tool applies the settled law from Magma General v. Nanu Ram and Satinder Kaur.

Several judgments in the corpus (doc_014, doc_028, doc_029) concern gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles — these are entirely inapposite to our facts and should not be confused with the third-party liability issue.

payload.holding: The petitions seeking quashing of criminal proceedings based on settlements in serious economic frauds and offences involving mental depravity are dismissed.

args.question: Motor accident claim by Mrs. Lakshmi Devi for death of spouse (aged 42, monthly income Rs 35,000, 3 dependants) involving a commercial truck driven without a valid driving licence. National Insurance Co. denies liability arguing policy void due to unlicensed driver.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot disown its statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 MV Act merely because the driver lacked an endorsement to drive a light motor vehicle as a commercial vehicle. The insurer must pay the third party and may recover from the insured if there was a breach.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim of a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab/taxi). The driver held an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to pay third-party compensation despite the licence defect.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent from the Supreme Court. It establishes that even where the driver's licence does not match the vehicle class (commercial vehicle), the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 remains intact. The insurer must pay and can only seek recovery from the owner.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of the offending tempo did not possess a valid driving licence. The Delhi High Court held the insurer statutorily liable to pay the third-party claimants and recover from the owner/driver.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly on point: the driver had no valid licence at all. The court confirmed that even a fundamental breach (invalid licence) does not defeat the third party's right to recover from the insurer. The insurer must pay first and then recover.
supporting.quote: The insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor either in the same proceedings or by independent proceedings as the case may be.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held only an LMV licence and lacked the badge/authorisation to drive a tourist Maxi Cab (commercial transport vehicle). The Madras High Court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Factually very close: a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab) driven by someone without the proper licence class. The court ordered pay-and-recover, confirming the insurer's liability to the third party.
supporting.quote: Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant... the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent - Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: An insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party award as a judgment debtor and recover from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion is established.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench of Karnataka High Court held that even fundamental breach does not defeat third-party rights. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench decision that comprehensively analyses the law. It confirms that the rule of pay-and-recover applies even for fundamental breaches, and the only exception is fraud/collusion between the victim and insured — which is not present here.
supporting.quote: The rule of pay and recover is applicable in view of the mandate in Section 149(4) of the Act and even if there is a breach of the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer is bound to satisfy the judgment and award as if it were a judgment debtor.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had an LMV/transport vehicle licence but not a heavy goods vehicle endorsement. The Madras High Court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the principle that licence class mismatch does not absolve the insurer of third-party liability. The court specifically rejected the insurer's argument that even pay-and-recover cannot be ordered.
supporting.quote: When the driver of the vehicle involved in the accident did not have a valid driving licence, whether the insurer can be directed to pay compensation to the Claimants and recover the same subsequently from the insured... [Answer: Yes].

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must pay the third party first and recover from the owner under the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver had no driving licence at all. The Tribunal found a fundamental breach but still ordered pay-and-recover to protect the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Even in the most extreme case — no licence whatsoever — the Tribunal ordered pay-and-recover. This is the worst-case scenario for the claimant on facts, and the court still protected the third party.
supporting.quote: The petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time... it is proper to direct the respondent No.2 to pay the compensation by reserving liberty to recover the same from the respondent No.1.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: Where a driver lacks a special endorsement required for the vehicle type (hazardous goods), the insurer cannot escape liability to third parties but has a right to recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for driving a tanker carrying hazardous goods. The Punjab & Haryana High Court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the licence defect is specific to the vehicle's use (commercial goods vehicle), the insurer's liability to third parties remains intact with recovery rights.
supporting.quote: The insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident. The Tribunal held the insurer liable, finding that non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach.
supporting.why_it_matters: The broader principle — that statutory liability to third parties overrides policy conditions — is directly applicable. Distinguishes between 'no licence' and 'licence expired' but the core principle holds.
supporting.quote: The liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy.

supporting.title: Surendra Singh And Another vs Vijay Singh And Another
supporting.principle: Multiplier must be based on deceased's age (not claimants'), future prospects apply to self-employed persons, and courts must award just compensation even without cross-appeal.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was 23 (here 42), self-employed. The court applied Sarla Verma multiplier table and Pranay Sethi future prospects percentages.
supporting.why_it_matters: Provides the quantum framework. For a 42-year-old self-employed deceased with 3 dependants: multiplier 14, future prospects 25%, 1/3rd deduction. This directly governs the compensation calculation.
supporting.quote: The multiplier to be used should be as mentioned in Column (4) of the table... which starts with an operative multiplier of 18... M-14 for 41 to 45 years.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver of the Tanker had no valid licence. The Allahabad High Court upheld the pay-and-recover order and also set aside a finding of contributory negligence.
supporting.why_it_matters: Directly supports the pay-and-recover principle for unlicensed drivers in commercial vehicles. Also helpful on the contributory negligence point — the court set aside a 50% contributory negligence finding based on assumptions from a site plan.
supporting.quote: Learned Tribunal though has accepted that there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker but even then has directed the insurance company to pay compensation to the claimants with a right to recover it from the owner.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period, but the insurer must still pay the third party and recover from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed after. The Karnataka High Court ordered pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Confirms that even where the licence was not valid on the date of accident (expired and renewed late), the insurer must still pay the third party and recover from the owner. Supports the pay-and-recover principle.
supporting.quote: Since it is the statutory right of the third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded either from the owner or the driver, as the vehicle in question is insured, the insurance company shall pay the amount and recover the same from driver or the insured.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks and does not extend to own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will cite this to argue that Swaran Singh's liberal approach is limited and that if the licence is fake (not merely absent), different considerations apply. They may try to conflate 'no licence' with 'fake licence' to argue the breach is more fundamental. However, the judgment expressly confines its holding to non-third-party claims.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment expressly limits its holding to non-third-party (own-damage) claims. It states: 'The decision in Swaran Singh's case has no application to cases other than third party risks.' Our client's claim is a third-party death claim, squarely within Swaran Singh's ambit. The 'fake licence' discussion is obiter for third-party claims and distinguishable — here the driver had no licence at all, not a fake one. The Supreme Court in S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and the consistent line of High Court decisions confirm that third-party claims are governed by the pay-and-recover principle regardless of licence defects.

adverse.title: Kamal S/O Shiv Ram vs Mursleem S/O Mohd. Akil
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence can constitute contributory negligence, reducing the claimant's compensation by 50%.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may argue that if the deceased himself was driving without a licence (if he was a driver/rider), contributory negligence applies. However, in our case the deceased was not driving — he was a pedestrian/third party killed by a commercial truck. This judgment is about an injured rider who was himself driving without a licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: In this case, the claimant himself was driving the motorcycle without a licence and without a helmet — his own negligence contributed to the accident. In our case, the deceased was an innocent third-party road user (pedestrian/other vehicle occupant) killed by a commercial truck. There is no allegation that the deceased contributed to the accident. The principle of contributory negligence has no application.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd., Thr ... vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
adverse.principle: Where a passenger travels in a private vehicle for hire or reward in breach of policy conditions, such passenger is not a 'third party' under the Act policy, and pay-and-recover cannot be ordered.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not available in all cases. However, this case is about passengers in a private vehicle for hire — a fundamentally different category from a third-party road user killed by a commercial truck.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns gratuitous passengers in a private vehicle — persons whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 147. Our client is a third-party road user (the deceased was not a passenger in the offending vehicle). The Supreme Court in Swaran Singh and S.Iyyapan has consistently held that third-party victims are entitled to recover from the insurer regardless of licence breaches. This judgment is inapplicable.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co.Ltd vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
adverse.principle: Where a risk is neither statutorily required to be covered nor covered under the policy (gratuitous passengers in goods vehicle), the Tribunal has no power under Section 149(4)/(5) to direct pay-and-recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is a limited remedy. But again, this concerns gratuitous passengers, not third-party road users.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The deceased was not a gratuitous passenger in the offending vehicle. He was a third-party road user killed by a commercial truck. The statutory requirement to insure third-party risks under Section 147 is mandatory and the insurer's liability to third parties is well-established. This judgment is confined to its facts about passengers in goods vehicles.

adverse.title: Dadapeera S/O Abdul Salam Sab vs Mallesh M S/O Hanumanthappa
adverse.principle: A person travelling on the mud-guard of a tractor is not covered by statutory insurance, and pay-and-recover cannot be granted for such persons who are not 'third parties'.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer may cite this to argue that pay-and-recover is not an absolute right and is limited to 'third parties'. However, our client is unquestionably a third party.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case concerns a person sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor — a person whose presence on the vehicle itself violates safety regulations. The court held such a person is not a 'third party'. Our client's deceased was a third-party road user, not a person riding on the offending vehicle. The distinction is fundamental and this judgment has no application.

priority_arguments: 1. STATUTORY LIABILITY TO THIRD PARTIES: The insurer's liability under Section 149 MV Act to third-party victims is statutory and cannot be defeated by a breach of policy conditions. Lead with S.Iyyapan (doc_032) and Satto (doc_033) — both hold that even where the driver had no valid licence, the insurer must pay the third party and recover from the owner.

2. PAY-AND-RECOVER IS THE ESTABLISHED REMEDY: Even if the insurer proves a fundamental breach (no licence), the consistent line of authority from the Supreme Court and High Courts mandates pay-and-recover. Cite Yallavva (doc_025, Full Bench), V.Vijayakumar (doc_035), Chennamma (doc_027), Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024), Meena (doc_006), and Parvathi Hebbar (doc_003).

3. BURDEN OF PROOF ON INSURER: The insurer must prove by cogent evidence that (a) the driver had no licence, AND (b) the owner was aware or complicit in the breach. Mere absence of a licence does not automatically absolve the insurer — the breach must be on the part of the insured (owner), not just the driver. Cite Swaran Singh principles as applied in Satto (doc_033).

4. QUANTUM: Deceased aged 42, self-employed, Rs 35,000/month, 3 dependants. Apply Sarla Verma multiplier of 14, future prospects at 25% (Pranay Sethi), 1/3rd deduction. Compute using the framework from Surendra Singh (doc_019). Estimated compensation: ~Rs 51 lakhs plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a.

5. NO COLLUSION OR FRAUD: The Full Bench in Yallavva (doc_025) held that the only exception to pay-and-recover is fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured. There is none here — the deceased was an innocent third-party road user.

6. NO CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE: The deceased was a third-party road user (not the driver). There is no basis for any contributory negligence argument. If the insurer raises it, cite Meena (doc_006) where the court set aside a 50% contributory negligence finding based on assumptions.
strategy.compensation_range: Rs 50,99,650 to Rs 52,95,650 (approximately Rs 51-53 lakhs) plus interest at 7.5-9% p.a. from the date of claim petition until realisation.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: Computed using compute_quantum tool: Monthly income Rs 35,000 → Annual Rs 4,20,000. Future prospects +25% (self-employed, age 42) → Rs 5,25,000. Less 1/3rd personal expenses (3 dependants) → Rs 3,50,000. Multiplier 14 (age 42) → Rs 49,00,000. Conventional heads: loss of estate Rs 19,965 + funeral Rs 19,965 + spousal consortium Rs 159,720 (wife) + parental consortium Rs 159,720 (2 minor children) = Rs 1,99,650. Total: Rs 50,99,650. Range reflects potential variation in future prospects percentage if employment status is disputed.
risks: The insurer may argue that the driver had no licence at all (not merely a mismatch of licence class), which some Tribunals have treated as a more serious breach. However, even in Sunil Shreesail Killiket (doc_024) where the driver had NO licence, pay-and-recover was ordered.

The insurer may argue that the owner (transport company) was complicit in allowing an unlicensed driver to operate a commercial vehicle, making this a 'conscious breach'. However, the consistent Supreme Court position is that even conscious/wilful breach does not defeat third-party rights — the insurer still pays and recovers (Satto doc_033, citing Lehru).
Risk that the Tribunal may reduce the multiplier or future prospects if the deceased's employment status (self-employed vs permanent) is disputed. Ensure documentary proof of income is produced.
The insurer may challenge the quantum by arguing that the income of Rs 35,000/month is not adequately proved. Ensure salary slips, bank statements, or income tax returns are available.

The insurer may attempt to argue that the deceased was a gratuitous passenger or not a third party — but this is factually impossible given the deceased was killed by a commercial truck while not riding in it.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is jointly and severally liable to pay the awarded compensation, with liberty to the insurer to recover the same from the owner/insured in separate proceedings. Alternatively, seek a direct pay-and-recover order. Given the clear line of authority, the claimant should also seek an order for interim compensation under Section 140 MV Act (no-fault liability) which is payable regardless of licence issues.

More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the Courts should keep in mind the objectives or
purpose for which statute has been enacted. Justice Frankfurter of U.S. Supreme Court in an article
titled as Some Reflections on the Reading of Statutes (47 Columbia Law Reports 527), observed that,
"legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change
of policy, to formulate a plan of Government. That aim, that policy is not drawn, like nitrogen, out of
the air; it is evidenced in the language of the statutes, as read in the light of other external
manifestations of purpose".

The inevitable conclusion therefore is that the decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no
application to own damage cases. The effect of fake license has to be considered in the light of what
has been stated by this Court in New India Assurance Co., Shimla v. Kamla and Ors. (2001 (4) SCC
342). Once the license is a fake one the renewal cannot take away the effect of fake license. It was
observed in Kamla's case (supra) as follows:
"12. As a point of law we have no manner of doubt that a fake licence cannot get its
forgery outfit stripped off merely on account of some officer renewing the same with
or without knowing it to be forged. Section 15 of the Act only empowers any Licensing
Authority to "renew a driving licence issued under the provisions of this Act with
effect from the date of its expiry". No Licensing Authority has the power to renew a
fake licence and, therefore, a renewal if at all made cannot transform a fake licence as
genuine. Any counterfeit document showing that it contains a purported order of a
statutory authority would ever remain counterfeit albeit the fact that other persons
including some statutory authorities would have acted on the document unwittingly
on the assumption that it is genuine".
As noted above, the conceptual difference between third party right and own damage cases has to be
kept in view. Initially, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the license was a fake one.

The primary stand of the insurance company is that the person driving the vehicle did not have a
valid driving license. In Swaran Singh's case (supra) the following situations were noted:
(i) the driver had a license but it was fake;

(ii) the driver had no license at all;
(iii) the driver originally had a valid license but it had expired as on the date of the
accident and had not been renewed;
(iv) the license was for a class of vehicles other than that which was the insured
vehicle;
(v) the license was a learner's license.
Category (i) may cover two types of situations. First, the license itself was fake and the second is
where originally that license is fake but there has been a renewal subsequently in accordance with
law.
Chapter II contains Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act relating to licensing of drivers driving the motor
vehicles.
Where the claim relates to own damage claims, it cannot be adjudicated by the insurance company.
But it has to be decided by an other forum i.e. forum created under the Consumer Protection Act,
1985 (in short the 'CP Act'). Before the Tribunal, there were essentially three parties i.e. the insurer,
insured and the claimants. On the contrary, before the consumer forums there were two parties i.e.
owner of the vehicle and the insurer. The claimant does not come in to the picture. Therefore, these
are cases where there is no third party involved.
According to learned counsel for the appellants, in such cases the logic i.e. let the insurer pay and
recover from the insured company does not apply.
As noted above, there is no contractual relation between the third party and the insurer. Because of
the statutory intervention in terms of Section 149, the same becomes operative in essence and
Section 149 provides complete insulation.
In the background of the statutory provisions, one thing is crystal clear i.e. the statute is beneficial
one qua the third party.

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr

The insurer must pay the third party and may recover from the insured if there was a breach.
supporting.fact_alignment: The deceased was a third-party victim of a commercial vehicle (Maxi Cab/taxi). The driver held an LMV licence but no commercial endorsement. The Supreme Court held the insurer liable to pay third-party compensation despite the licence defect.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest supporting precedent from the Supreme Court. It establishes that even where the driver's licence does not match the vehicle class (commercial vehicle), the insurer's statutory liability to third parties under Section 149 remains intact. The insurer must pay and can only seek recovery from the owner.
supporting.quote: In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd

However, the consistent Supreme Court position is that even conscious/wilful breach does not defeat third-party rights — the insurer still pays and recovers (Satto doc_033, citing Lehru).
Risk that the Tribunal may reduce the multiplier or future prospects if the deceased's employment status (self-employed vs permanent) is disputed. Ensure documentary proof of income is produced.
The insurer may challenge the quantum by arguing that the income of Rs 35,000/month is not adequately proved. Ensure salary slips, bank statements, or income tax returns are available.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: File claim under Section 166 MV Act before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place of accident. Seek a declaration that the insurer is jointly and severally liable to pay the awarded compensation, with liberty to the insurer to recover the same from the owner/insured in separate proceedings. Alternatively, seek a direct pay-and-recover order. Given the clear line of authority, the claimant should also seek an order for interim compensation under Section 140 MV Act (no-fault liability) which is payable regardless of licence issues.
